newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania may explode if pyramids tumble -experts.
newsitem.headline: Albania may explode if pyramids tumble -experts.

text.p: Albanian pyramid schemes are falling like dominoes and when the last one tumbles the country risks being engulfed in violence, commentators and opposition parties said on Wednesday.

Sporadic rioting has broken out across the Balkan state in recent weeks after the collapse of a number of the get-rich-quick investment schemes, but the protests were capped by a swift police crackdown and the fear of long jail terms.

Some of the most popular pyramids are still clinging to life, but many economists believe these too are doomed to die, and when that happens the ruling right-wing Democratic Party will struggle to suppress public anger.
"When you are dealing with money you can't keep Albanians intimidated for long," Rexhep Mejdani, the leader of the main opposition Socialist party, told Reuters.

As much as $2 billion might be invested in pyramid schemes which blossomed across post-communist Albania, according to local people. Refunds are being organised for some funds, but many people risk financial ruin.
"You can intimidate people for a day, a week or a month... but I'm afraid in the end they will explode," Mejdani said.
Commentators said that if the explosion comes it might be compounded by the lack of a strong figure to oppose the government, blamed by many for not stopping the astonishing growth of the pyramids.

The main opposition groups joined forces last week in a "Forum for Democracy" to press for the resignation of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi, but the alliance lacks a charismatic leader and is perceived to be deeply divided.
"The opposition is not capable of controlling the protests or channelling the anger," said Ben Blushi, editor-in-chief of the anti-government daily Koha Jone, the biggest in Albania.
"Unless the opposition gets better organised the people will find their own leader and that could be dangerous...I'm afraid the crowds will end up very violent," he added.

Police arrested nearly 150 people after the first wave of protests last month and rioters are threatened with a minimum of 15 years in prison. Meksi has denied widespread rumours that his government profited from the pyramids.

A local businessman who declined to be named said many people in impoverished Albania had stayed away from protests in the hope that the remaining pyramid and investment schemes would continue paying out interest.

However, these hopes took a knock on Tuesday when the head of the second-largest fund, Gjallica, which owed up to $500 million, announced he was bankrupt. The news sparked a mass demonstration in the southern port city of Vlores.

"When the remaining pyramids fall, as they are bound to, then we will have economic collapse and protests that won't be nearly as civilised as the demonstrations in Belgrade and Sofia," the middle-aged businessman said.
Yugoslavia and Bulgaria have witnessed huge, mainly peaceful protests in recent weeks which have forced concessions from their respective governments.
President Sali Berisha, who founded the Democratic Party and helped bury the old communist elite, has divided the opposition and subdued student and union movements.
The former head of the Socialist party, Fatos Nano, was imprisoned in 1994 on corruption charges in a move criticised by international human rights groups.
"He was the only opposition leader to have charisma and Berisha has profited from his arrest," Blushi said.
The Tirana businessman called on the international community to put pressure on Berisha to form a cross-party alliance to try to resolve the growing crisis.
"We have a very tense situation here and it's only going to get worse," he said.
